Corn (Maize) with Cercospora and Gray Le.model_class_id: Corn (Maize) with Cercospora and Gray Leaf Spot
Corn (Maize) with Cercospora and Gray Le.description: A fungal foliar disease in maize favored by warm, humid weather and prolonged leaf wetness, causing rectangular lesions along leaf veins.
symptoms: Small, tan spots that elongate into narrow rectangular brown-gray lesions
Lesions bounded by leaf veins with distinct parallel edges
Severe blighting and premature drying of lower canopy leaves
treatment: Consult a local agricultural extension officer to verify local severity thresholds before considering chemical intervention.
Avoid handling or cultivating through wet crop foliage to reduce spore dispersal.
Remove heavily infected residue from small plots after harvest.
prevention: Plant certified tolerant or resistant maize varieties recommended for your agro-ecological zone.
Rotate with non-host crops (such as legumes, cowpea, or soybean) to interrupt disease carryover in crop debris.
Ensure proper planting density to promote air movement and reduce canopy humidity.
sources: CIMMYT - Maize Diseases: A Guide for Field Identification
IITA - Research Guide: Maize Pathology and Crop Protection

Corn (Maize) with Common Rust.description: A airborne fungal disease causing powdery cinnamon-brown pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces.
symptoms: Oval to elongate cinnamon-brown pustules scattered across both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the leaf epidermis to release powdery orange-brown spores
Chlorosis and drying of severely infected leaf tissue
treatment: Consult local agricultural extension agents for guidance if pustules appear before tassel emergence.
Maintain balanced plant nutrition to help the crop withstand foliar stress.
Avoid overhead irrigation where practical.
prevention: Plant locally adapted, rust-resistant hybrid or open-pollinated maize seed.
Time planting with regional extension calendars to avoid peak spore migration windows.
Practice clean field borders and weed control.
sources: CIMMYT - Maize Diseases: A Guide for Field Identification
FAO - Integrated Pest Management for Maize

Corn (Maize) with Northern Leaf Blight.description: A serious fungal foliar blighting disease that produces long, elliptical grayish-green lesions on maize foliage.
symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped elliptical lesions (2.5 to 15 cm long) on leaves
Lesions start grayish-green and mature into tan or brown with dark spore margins
Extensive leaf tissue death when multiple lesions coalesce
treatment: Contact an extension agronomist to assess field incidence before silking stage.
Avoid sprinkler or overhead wetting during warm humid periods.
Collect and bury or burn heavily blighted residue post-harvest if practical.
prevention: Select resistant or tolerant maize seed cultivars verified by regional seed boards.
Practice minimum two-year crop rotation with non-grass crops (e.g. cowpea, soybean, groundnut).
Incorporate or decompose surface crop residues that harbor overwintering fungal structures.
sources: IITA - Maize Production and Disease Management Manual
CIMMYT - Field Guide to Maize Diseases

Healthy Corn (Maize) Plant.description: No visible leaf disease symptoms detected. The foliage exhibits uniform green coloration with normal vein architecture.
symptoms: Uniform green leaves without lesions, pustules, or chlorotic streaks
Clean leaf edges and upright, vigorous growth
Intact leaf surface free of fungal sporulation
treatment: No disease treatment needed.
Maintain regular crop scouting every 7 to 10 days to monitor for emergence of pests or spots.
prevention: Continue standard good agronomic practices including timely weeding and balanced fertilization.
Monitor soil moisture and maintain good field drainage.
Report any sudden change in leaf color or spot emergence to local extension officers.
sources: IITA - Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) for Maize
FAO - Crop Management Guidelines

Orange with Citrus Greening.description: A devastating, insect-vectored bacterial disease of citrus that causes asymmetrical leaf mottling, twig dieback, and small, misshapen, bitter fruit.
symptoms: Asymmetrical blotchy mottle on leaves crossing leaf veins
Yellowing of veins followed by yellow shoot development
Small, lopsided fruit that remain green at the bottom and taste bitter
Twig dieback and progressive tree decline
treatment: Immediately report suspected cases to national plant protection agencies or local extension authorities.
There is no known cure for infected trees; infected trees should be removed and destroyed as advised by agricultural authorities to protect neighboring orchards.
Do not move plant material, scions, or nursery stock from suspected infected areas.
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free nursery stock from inspected, registered citrus nurseries.
Monitor orchards for the presence of psyllid insect vectors (Diaphorina citri or Trioza erytreae).
Manage psyllid vector populations following official regional pest management advisories.
sources: FAO - Citrus Greening Disease Technical Manual
EPPO / IITA - Plant Quarantine and Citrus Health Briefs

Bell Pepper with Bacterial Spot.description: A bacterial disease favored by warm temperatures and heavy rainfall that causes water-soaked spots on leaves and scabby lesions on fruit.
symptoms: Small, circular to irregular water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown-black with pale halos
Spots may crack or drop out, giving leaves a ragged look
Severe defoliation exposing developing fruit to sunscald
Rough, raised, warty lesions on pepper fruit
treatment: Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base of the plant to prevent splashing bacteria.
Refrain from working in or weeding pepper rows while foliage is wet from rain or dew.
Remove and destroy severely affected plant debris away from production beds.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds or hot-water treated seeds.
Select resistant pepper cultivars where available.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (avoid planting after tomato, potato, or eggplant) for at least two years.
Disinfect stakes, trays, and cutting tools with appropriate cleaning solutions.
sources: World Vegetable Center (WorldVeg) - Pepper Diseases and Management
FAO - Integrated Pest Management for Solanaceous Crops

Healthy Bell Pepper Plant.description: No disease symptoms observed. Foliage is firm, uniformly colored, and growing vigorously.
symptoms: Clean, smooth green leaves free of spots, blisters, or curling
Sturdy stem and vigorous branching
Normal flower and fruit set without surface lesions
treatment: No treatment required.
Continue routine weekly field monitoring for signs of pests or bacterial lesions.
prevention: Maintain consistent soil moisture and avoid waterlogging around roots.
Apply organic mulch to retain moisture and prevent soil splash.
Practice balanced crop nutrition and avoid excess nitrogen which causes soft, disease-prone growth.
sources: WorldVeg - Good Agricultural Practices for Sweet Pepper
IITA - Vegetable Guide

Potato with Early Blight.description: A common fungal disease of potato causing dark, concentric target-like spots primarily on older leaves.
symptoms: Small dark brown to black spots with concentric rings (target pattern) on older leaves
Yellowing of leaf tissue surrounding the spots
Leaves turn brown, wither, and drop prematurely as spots enlarge
treatment: Consult local extension services for approved regional management protocols.
Prune and safely dispose of heavily infected lower leaves in small gardens.
Irrigate early in the morning so leaf surfaces dry rapidly during the day.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (such as maize, legumes, or sorghum) for 2 to 3 years.
Maintain adequate plant nutrition, especially nitrogen and potassium, to prevent plant stress.
Destroy volunteer potato plants and cull piles near fields.
sources: International Potato Center (CIP) - Potato Pathology Manual
FAO - Integrated Pest Management for Potato

Potato with Late Blight.description: A destructive water mold (oomycete) pathogen that rapidly blights leaves, stems, and tubers under cool, moist conditions.
symptoms: Water-soaked dark green to purplish-black lesions on leaves and stems
White fungal-like fuzzy growth on the underside of leaves during humid conditions
Rapid wilting, browning, and rotting of foliage within days
Dry, brownish granular rot beneath tuber skin
treatment: Immediately notify extension agents if late blight is suspected in your locality.
Destroy heavily diseased plants immediately to prevent airborne spore clouds from spreading.
Avoid overhead watering and do not wash harvested tubers from infected plots.
prevention: Plant certified resistant or tolerant potato varieties.
Ensure proper hilling of soil over potato beds to prevent spores washing down to tubers.
Strictly destroy cull piles and volunteer potatoes before the planting season.
Never save seed tubers from fields affected by late blight.
sources: International Potato Center (CIP) - Late Blight Management Guide
FAO - Potato Pest and Disease Compendium

Healthy Potato Plant.description: No visible signs of foliar disease. Foliage displays healthy green development.
symptoms: Lush, uniformly green leaves with clean surfaces
Sturdy upright stems without lesions or dark cankers
Healthy root and stolon formation without decay
treatment: No treatment required.
Conduct regular weekly scouting, particularly during cool, misty, or rainy periods.
prevention: Keep soil properly hilled around stems to shield developing tubers from sunlight and spore exposure.
Maintain consistent, well-drained soil moisture.
Follow clean tool sanitation when moving between plots.
sources: International Potato Center (CIP) - Potato Production Guide
FAO - Good Agricultural Practices for Root and Tuber Crops

Tomato with Bacterial Spot.description: A bacterial pathogen causing small, dark, water-soaked spots on tomato foliage, stems, and fruit.
symptoms: Small, dark brown to black water-soaked lesions on leaves and stems
Spots may have a greasy appearance and can be surrounded by yellow halos
Severe infection leads to leaf yellowing, scorch, and heavy defoliation
Small, scabby, slightly raised black spots on immature fruit
treatment: Remove heavily infected leaves in small holdings; do not work in fields when foliage is wet.
Consult extension workers for locally registered preventative sprays if disease pressure is high.
Water at ground level using drip or furrow methods to minimize splash dispersal.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds from reputable suppliers.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for at least 2 consecutive years.
Clean and sanitize greenhouse benches, stakes, and pruning shears.
sources: World Vegetable Center (WorldVeg) - Tomato Disease Management
FAO - Integrated Pest Management for Tomato

Tomato with Early Blight.description: Fungal disease characterized by concentric dark brown target-like rings on older lower leaves, eventually causing yellowing and premature leaf drop.
symptoms: Small brown-black spots on older lower leaves that enlarge into concentric target rings
Yellow halos surrounding individual spots
Progressive yellowing, withering, and dropping of lower leaves
Sunken, dark, leathery lesions at the stem end of fruits
treatment: Prune and dispose of infected lower leaves immediately; do not compost them.
Ensure foliage remains dry when watering; switch to drip or root-level watering.
Consult local extension officers for approved regional fungal management guidelines.
prevention: Practice 2 to 3-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops.
Apply clean straw or organic mulch around plant bases to prevent soil splash.
Space plants at least 50–60 cm apart to promote good air circulation.
Stake tomato vines to keep foliage off bare ground.
sources: IITA - Tomato Production and Pest Management Manual
WorldVeg - Integrated Disease Management in Tomato

Tomato with Late Blight.description: A fast-spreading water mold that causes large water-soaked spots, rapid leaf collapse, and firm, dark brown fruit rot in cool, humid conditions.
symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked pale-green to brown lesions on leaves and stems
White fungal-like fuzz on lesion undersides during humid morning hours
Rapid blighting and collapse of entire vines within days
Large, firm, greasy brown lesions on green and ripening fruit
treatment: Remove and destroy severely blighted plants immediately; do not leave them in the field.
Notify nearby growers and agricultural extension officers, as late blight spores travel on wind currents.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation.
prevention: Plant certified resistant varieties where available.
Avoid planting tomatoes adjacent to potato fields.
Ensure wide spacing and staking to maximize canopy airflow.
Eliminate cull piles, volunteer tomatoes, and solanaceous weeds near production fields.
sources: FAO - Integrated Pest Management for Tomato
IITA - Plant Health and Vegetable Guide

Tomato with Leaf Mold.description: A fungal disease prevalent in high humidity and enclosed spaces (like greenhouses or high tunnels), producing pale green-yellow spots with velvety olive-brown mold beneath.
symptoms: Pale green to yellowish patches on upper surfaces of older leaves
Dense olive-green to brownish velvety mold growth on the lower leaf surface corresponding to spots
Affected leaves turn yellow, curl, and wither, reducing plant photosynthesis
treatment: Improve ventilation and lower relative humidity in enclosed growing structures.
Prune lower foliage to increase air circulation through the canopy.
Avoid wetting the foliage during irrigation.
prevention: Select tomato cultivars with known resistance to leaf mold races.
Maintain adequate plant spacing (at least 60 cm between plants).
Sanitize greenhouse structures, stakes, and tools between crop cycles.
sources: WorldVeg - Tomato Disease Identification Guide
FAO - Protected Agriculture Pest Management

Tomato with Septoria Leaf Spot.description: A fungal disease causing numerous small, circular spots with dark margins and grayish centers on lower tomato leaves.
symptoms: Numerous small (1.5 to 3 mm), circular spots on lower leaves
Spots feature dark brown borders and grayish-white centers with tiny black speckles (pycnidia)
Leaves turn yellow, dry out, and drop prematurely, progressing upwards from plant base
treatment: Pinch off and discard infected lower leaves as soon as first spots appear.
Water exclusively at soil level using drip systems.
Consult extension agents for approved protective sprays if defoliation threatens fruit yield.
prevention: Rotate fields away from solanaceous crops for 2 or more years.
Apply organic mulch around vines to prevent soil-splashed spores.
Stake and prune plants to promote sunlight penetration and leaf drying.
Clean up all tomato crop residue after harvest.
sources: IITA - Vegetable Guide: Disease Management
WorldVeg - Tomato Pathology Compendium

Tomato with Spider Mites or Two-spotted.model_class_id: Tomato with Spider Mites or Two-spotted Spider Mite
Tomato with Spider Mites or Two-spotted.description: Tiny arachnid pests that feed by piercing leaf cells under hot, dry conditions, causing pale stippling and fine webbing on leaf undersides.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling (pinpoint dots) on upper leaf surfaces
Silken, delicate webbing visible on leaf undersides and terminal shoots
Leaves turn bronze or yellow, dry up, and drop in severe infestations
Overall stunted plant growth and reduced fruit size
treatment: Spray leaf undersides with strong streams of water to dislodge mites in small plots.
Conserve natural predators (such as predatory mites and ladybugs) by avoiding indiscriminate broad-spectrum sprays.
Consult local extension officers for approved horticultural oils or soaps.
prevention: Avoid water stress by maintaining consistent soil moisture, as mites thrive in drought-stressed crops.
Control weeds and dust along field borders.
Inspect leaf undersides weekly with a hand lens during hot dry seasons.
sources: FAO - Integrated Pest Management for Tomato
IITA - Insect Pests of Horticultural Crops

Tomato with Target Spot.description: A fungal foliar disease favored by warm, humid environments, causing brown circular spots that may develop faint concentric rings.
symptoms: Small, pinpoint water-soaked spots on upper leaf surfaces
Lesions enlarge into circular brown lesions with light brown centers and faint concentric zones
Severe leaf blighting, premature yellowing, and defoliation
Small brown lesions on green and ripe fruit
treatment: Remove and safely discard diseased foliage in small plots.
Improve air movement by thinning excess vegetative suckers.
Seek advice from extension officers if target spot spreads through the upper canopy.
prevention: Rotate out of solanaceous and cucurbit crops that also host Corynespora.
Stake vines and maintain 50 to 60 cm in-row spacing.
Avoid overhead irrigation and keep field borders clean of weed hosts.
sources: WorldVeg - Diagnostic Guide to Tomato Target Spot
FAO - IPM Solanaceous Factsheets

Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus.description: A severe viral disease transmitted by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) that causes severe stunting, upward leaf curling, and drastic fruit yield reduction.
symptoms: Pronounced upward curling and cupping of leaflet margins
Interveinal yellowing (chlorosis) of younger leaves
Marked plant stunting with a bushy, erect appearance
Severe drop of flowers and little to no fruit set on early-infected plants
treatment: There is no cure for viral infection; promptly rogue (uproot and bury/burn) early infected plants to remove the virus reservoir.
Manage the whitefly vector population following extension recommendations (e.g. yellow sticky traps, insect exclusion netting in nurseries).
Keep surrounding areas free of alternate weed hosts.
prevention: Plant certified TYLCV-resistant or tolerant tomato hybrids.
Protect seedlings in nurseries with fine insect-proof mesh netting (50-mesh) before transplanting.
Avoid planting new tomato fields downwind from older, infested tomato or pepper fields.
Implement a host-free fallow period between cropping seasons.
sources: IITA - Whitefly-Transmitted Viruses and Management in West Africa
WorldVeg - Management of Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus Disease

Tomato Mosaic Virus.description: A persistent, mechanically transmitted plant virus causing mottled green and yellow patterns, leaf distortion, and stunted growth.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green patterns on leaves ('mosaic' appearance)
Distortion, puckering, or 'shoestringing' of leaflets
Plant stunting and internal browning of fruit walls
Uneven ripening and reduced fruit quality
treatment: Immediately rogue and discard infected plants; do not compost them.
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and clean water after handling infected crops or tobacco products.
Disinfect all cutting tools, stakes, and crates with clean water and disinfectant.
prevention: Plant certified virus-free seed or resistant tomato cultivars.
Prohibit smoking or handling raw tobacco near tomato beds, as tobacco can carry the related Tobacco Mosaic Virus.
Practice strict field hygiene and sanitize tools before moving between rows.
sources: WorldVeg - Viral Diseases of Tomato
FAO - Integrated Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetables

Healthy Tomato Plant.description: No visible foliar disease symptoms detected. Foliage displays vigorous, uniform green growth with normal leaf shape.
symptoms: Uniform deep green foliage without spots, curling, or yellow halos
Strong central stem with well-developed branches
Healthy flower trusses and smooth, clean developing fruit
treatment: No disease treatment required.
Continue regular weekly scouting of upper and lower leaf surfaces.
prevention: Maintain consistent soil moisture using drip irrigation or soil-level watering.
Apply organic mulch around plant bases to suppress weeds and retain soil moisture.
Stake vines and prune lower suckers to promote good air circulation.
sources: IITA - Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) for Tomato Production
FAO - Vegetable Production Guidelines
